result: Nodal-deficient zebrafish gastrulae (MZoep mutants) exhibit severely disrupted convergence and extension (C&E) cell behaviors in the neuroectoderm, including disorganized cell movements, reduced mediolateral (ML) and anteroposterior (AP) displacement, decreased cell elongation and alignment, and randomized cellular protrusions. These defects require Nodal signaling in both cell-autonomous and non-autonomous fashions, as demonstrated by transplantation experiments showing partial rescue of MZoep mutant cell alignment in wild-type hosts.
evaluation: Claims C5-C58 and C63 are well-supported by comprehensive quantitative analyses including automated cell tracking (Figure 1B-G), morphometric measurements of cell shape and alignment (Figure 1H-J), and protrusion orientation analysis (Figure 1L-M), all with appropriate statistical tests (p<0.0001). Transplantation experiments (Figure 1K-N) provide direct evidence for both autonomous and non-autonomous roles, with MZoep cells showing intermediate alignment when transplanted into WT hosts compared to MZoep hosts.

result: PCP signaling remains partially active in Nodal-deficient embryos, as evidenced by similar proportions of anteriorly localized Prickle-GFP in MZoep mutants compared to wild-type. Genetic interaction experiments demonstrate that disrupting PCP signaling via vangl2 morpholino exacerbates C&E defects in MZoep mutants, indicating that Nodal does not regulate C&E solely through PCP and that PCP is not strictly downstream of Nodal.
evaluation: Claims C7-C70 are supported by Prickle-GFP localization data (Figure 2A-B, p=0.0001), cell alignment measurements in double-perturbation experiments (Figure 2C-D), and neural plate morphometry showing additive effects of Nodal loss and PCP inhibition (Figure 2E-G, p<0.0001). RNA-seq data (Figure 2—supplement 1) confirms that most PCP genes are expressed normally in MZoep mutants, supporting the interpretation that PCP functions partially independently of Nodal.

result: Nodal signaling is sufficient to induce robust convergence and extension in naïve zebrafish blastoderm explants in a dose-dependent manner. Injection of ndr2 mRNA (2.5-100 pg) induces explant extension beginning at ~8 hpf, with intermediate doses (5-25 pg, optimal at 10 pg) producing the most extension. These explants exhibit organized cell movements characteristic of C&E and express tissue-specific markers (endoderm, mesoderm, neuroectoderm) in discrete, spatially organized domains according to Nodal dose.
evaluation: Claims C71-C91 are well-supported by morphological observations (Figure 3B-F), automated cell tracking showing organized ML and AP displacement patterns (Figure 3G-K), and comprehensive WISH analysis demonstrating dose-dependent tissue specification (Figure 3L, Figure 3—supplement 1). The explant system provides appropriate controls (GFP-injected, uninjected, and MZoep mutant explants all fail to extend), and time-lapse imaging confirms the timing of extension onset corresponds to intact embryos.

result: Nodal-expressing explants exhibit asymmetric Nodal signaling activity along the axis of extension, as demonstrated by asymmetric distribution of phosphorylated Smad2-positive nuclei beginning at 6 hpf and increasing until 8 hpf (p<0.0001), and by asymmetric expression of the Nodal target gene lefty1. This asymmetry develops despite uniform injection of ndr2 mRNA at the one-cell stage.
evaluation: Claims C92-C104 are supported by quantitative 3D analysis of pSmad2 immunofluorescence using automated object detection (Figure 4A-C, p<0.0001, K-S tests) and WISH for lefty1 (Figure 4D). The specificity of the pSmad2 antibody is validated by SB-505124 treatment controls (Figure 4—supplement 1). The timing differences between explants and intact embryos are documented and acknowledged. However, the mechanism generating asymmetry from uniform mRNA injection remains unexplained.

result: Nodal-induced convergence and extension in explants is largely PCP-dependent. Nodal-expressing explants exhibit robust ML cell alignment (median angle 19° from ML), while control explants show random orientation (median angle 44°). Disruption of PCP signaling via vangl2 morpholino significantly reduces but does not eliminate explant extension and cell alignment, indicating that PCP functions downstream of Nodal in the explant context.
evaluation: Claims C9 and C105-C115 are supported by quantitative cell alignment measurements (Figure 5A,C) and morphometric analysis of explant dimensions (Figure 5B,D,E, p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test). The partial rather than complete loss of extension in vangl2 morphants is consistent with incomplete knockdown or additional PCP-independent mechanisms. The interpretation that PCP functions downstream of Nodal ex vivo is logically sound given that control explants show no extension or polarity, while Nodal-induced polarity is reduced by PCP inhibition.

result: Nodal signaling contributes to explant extension after mesoderm specification and even in the absence of mesoderm. Treatment with the Nodal inhibitor SB-505124 at 8 hpf (after mesoderm formation) significantly reduces extension despite robust mesoderm marker expression (p<0.0001). Pulse treatment from 6-8 hpf blocks mesoderm formation but allows subsequent neuroectoderm extension, demonstrating a tissue-autonomous, mesoderm-independent role for Nodal in C&E.
evaluation: Claims C119-C131 and C154-C155 are supported by well-designed temporal inhibitor experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 6). The use of WISH for mesoderm markers (tbxta, noto, tbx16) and neuroectoderm markers (sox2, otx2b) provides clear evidence for tissue identity (Figure 6E, Figure 6—supplement 2). Quantitative morphometry with statistical analysis (p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test) supports the conclusion that Nodal functions after mesoderm specification. The washout experiments elegantly demonstrate that neural-only explants can extend, though the reduced extension compared to controls suggests mesoderm does contribute.

result: Nodal acts both upstream of and in parallel with PCP during gastrulation to regulate embryonic axis extension cooperatively. In vivo, Nodal and PCP are each necessary but not sufficient for full ML polarization, with PCP remaining partially active in Nodal-deficient embryos. Ex vivo, PCP functions wholly downstream of Nodal. Additional Nodal-independent mechanisms (likely AP patterning cues) are proposed to polarize PCP signaling in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C10, C134-C142, C151-C152, and C164-C166 represent the central interpretive model of the manuscript, synthesizing results from in vivo and ex vivo experiments. The model is well-supported by the combined evidence: (1) MZoep mutants retain partial PCP activity and cell polarity (Figure 2), (2) PCP inhibition worsens MZoep phenotypes (Figure 2), (3) Nodal is sufficient for polarity ex vivo (Figures 3-5), and (4) PCP inhibition reduces Nodal-induced polarity ex vivo (Figure 5). The proposal of additional signals ('X') is speculative but reasonable given that PCP is polarized in MZoep mutants. The model is clearly depicted in Figure 7.

result: Transplantation experiments demonstrate both cell-autonomous and non-autonomous requirements for Nodal in ML cell polarization. MZoep mutant cells in wild-type hosts show significantly better alignment than MZoep cells in MZoep hosts (p<0.0001) but significantly worse alignment than wild-type control donors (p<0.0001), indicating partial rescue by the wild-type environment.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by quantitative cell alignment measurements from transplantation experiments (Figure 1N) with appropriate statistical analysis (K-S tests, p<0.0001). The intermediate phenotype of mutant cells in wild-type hosts provides clear evidence for both autonomous and non-autonomous functions. However, there is some inconsistency noted in the manuscript regarding the 8.5 hpf timepoint between different experimental series (Figure 1N vs Figure 2D), which the authors acknowledge but does not fundamentally undermine the conclusion.

result: Cell proliferation is not likely to be a major driver of convergence and extension morphogenesis in zebrafish gastrulae or explants, as cell divisions are relatively infrequent during the relevant time window and are not concentrated in regions that would drive directional extension.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by manual annotation of cell divisions in explants (Figure 3—supplement 2) showing modest division rates and distribution along rather than concentrated at specific regions of the extension axis. This is consistent with prior literature in intact embryos (Liu et al., 2017) and recent explant studies (Schauer et al., 2020) showing that blocking divisions does not prevent extension. The evidence is sufficient to support the negative claim that proliferation is not a major driver.

result: Nodal may contribute to polarized cell behaviors through additional PCP-independent mechanisms, and/or vangl2 knockdown may not completely abolish all PCP signaling modules. The incomplete loss of polarity in vangl2 morphant explants suggests either additional Nodal effectors or the modular nature of PCP signaling.
evaluation: Claims C143-C144 and C148-C149 are speculative interpretations based on the observation that vangl2 morphant explants retain some extension and polarity (Figure 5). While the data clearly show incomplete loss of function, distinguishing between incomplete knockdown versus additional mechanisms requires further experimentation. The discussion of PCP modularity is supported by literature citations (C145-C147) but the specific application to Nodal regulation remains hypothetical. This represents an important area for future investigation but cannot be definitively resolved with the current data.

result: Zebrafish animal-most blastoderm explants provide a robust, simplified model of axial extension in which Nodal can be studied independently of endogenous patterning signals. These explants are comparatively naïve (excluding margin signals) and fail to extend without exogenous Nodal, yet exhibit biologically relevant behaviors including C&E movements, ML cell polarization, appropriate timing, and transcriptional responses.
evaluation: Claims C156-C163 describe the explant system and its validation. The characterization is well-supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript and by appropriate citations to prior literature. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations of the system (C161-C162) including absence of the full complement of signals and altered geometry without the yolk cell. The claim that explants exhibit behaviors in common with intact embryos is supported by the timing, cell behavior, and gene expression data presented in Figures 3-6.

result: Background claims establishing the scientific context for the study, including the roles of convergence and extension movements, PCP signaling, Nodal signaling, and their known functions in vertebrate gastrulation based on prior literature.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C11-C43 are background statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide the necessary context for the experimental work and accurately represent the state of knowledge in the field. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with the cited work. These are not novel findings of this manuscript but rather establish the rationale for the investigation.

result: Additional background claims from the Discussion section, including prior models for Nodal function in axis extension, the role of mesoderm, mechanical cues in planar polarity, and the modular nature of PCP signaling, all supported by citations to previous literature.
evaluation: Claims C116-C118, C132-C133, C145-C147, C150, and C153 are background statements from the Discussion that accurately represent prior work and provide context for interpreting the current findings. These are appropriately cited and help frame the significance of the new results. They are not novel findings but rather establish how the current work relates to and extends previous models.
